query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys designed for high-temperature applications, the oxidation resistance is due to the formation of a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer. This protective layer forms because the high-entropy matrix slows down diffusion, causing selective enrichment of elements with high oxygen affinity (specifically Cr and Ta) at the surface, which then react to form a stable oxide barrier that blocks further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy containing Cr, Ta, and other alloying elements (e.g., as used in RHEAs) with no pre-existing oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to long-term high-temperature isothermal oxidation (e.g., at 1100°C for up to 200 hours) under identical conditions. In a controlled comparison, test an alloy having optimized Cr and Ta content against a variant with reduced levels of these key elements.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air under isothermal conditions. The experiment compares the full alloy (with full Cr and Ta content) to a control alloy where Cr and/or Ta are reduced, to assess the role of selective element enrichment and oxide layer formation.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer on the alloy surface, whose integrity is maintained by the sluggish diffusion kinetics inherent to the high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The high-entropy matrix impedes diffusion, leading to a selective surface enrichment of Cr and Ta that have high oxygen affinities. These elements rapidly oxidize to form a continuous CrTaO4-based layer. This layer serves as a kinetic barrier to further oxygen ingress, thereby slowing subsequent oxidation. Without the sluggish diffusion typical of HEAs, the selective oxidation would be less efficient, leading to a more porous, non-protective scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with full Cr and Ta content will develop a well-adhered, laminated oxide scale with an initial mixed oxide layer that transitions to a continuous, protective CrTaO4-based layer, resulting in significantly lower mass gain (e.g., a parabolic oxidation behavior with low weight gain) relative to the control alloy. The control alloy (with reduced Cr and/or Ta) is predicted to exhibit non-protective, porous oxide formation with exponential mass gain and a higher overall oxidation rate.
generation.baseline: The control high-entropy alloy variant with reduced Cr and/or Ta content should show a non-protective oxide scale and higher oxidation rate (e.g., an exponential weight gain versus parabolic kinetics in the full alloy), demonstrating less oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected in refractory high-entropy alloys exposed to prolonged high-temperature oxidation (around and above 1000°C). The hypothesis may not apply if grain coarsening, phase segregation, or extreme environmental factors (e.g., very high oxygen pressures or corrosive atmospheres) alter the oxidation kinetics or oxide scale stability.
generation.uncertainty: Exact diffusion coefficients and the quantitative kinetics of selective element segregation in the high-entropy matrix are not fully characterized. Additionally, the influence of secondary alloying elements on oxide formation and long-term scale adherence introduces some uncertainty in precisely predicting oxide growth rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy alloys: one with standard levels of Cr and Ta (the full alloy) and a variant with significantly reduced Cr and/or Ta. Subject both alloys to the same isothermal oxidation treatment at 1100°C for 200 hours in air. Use identical sample preparation and testing protocols to ensure a fair direct comparison.
measurements: Mass gain measurements (thermogravimetric analysis) over time to determine oxidation kinetics
Surface morphology and cross-sectional analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase identification and oxide scale composition via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Elemental mapping (EDS) to verify selective enrichment of Cr and Ta at the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the full alloy (with normal Cr and Ta levels) does not show a lower mass gain and fails to form a continuous, protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer – that is, if its oxidation kinetics, oxide layer morphology, and elemental distribution are similar to those of the reduced Cr/Ta variant – then the hypothesis is falsified.

Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C

Abstract: AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
